lead: Cruise control keeps a car at a speed the driver chooses, without the driver holding the pedal. It measures actual speed, compares it with the set speed, and moves the throttle through a controller. Adaptive cruise control (ACC) adds a forward sensor: it also measures the gap to the car ahead and slows or brakes to keep a safe time gap. Used on highways, in stop-and-go traffic, and in many new cars sold in India with radar or camera systems.
prereq: You need: how throttle changes engine torque (electronic engine control), radar and wheel speed sensors (automotive sensors and actuators), and electronic transmission control for how a controller commands an actuator.

blocks.text: Basic cruise control holds a driver-chosen speed. The driver presses SET above a minimum speed, often around 30 km/h. The controller stores the set speed v<sub>set</sub>. RESUME brings back the stored speed after a cancel. CANCEL or a tap on the brake ends control. Holding COAST closes the throttle so the car slows; when the button is released, the speed reached is stored as the new v<sub>set</sub>. Actual speed v comes from wheel speed sensors.
e = vset − v; u = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt

e is speed error in m/s; v<sub>set</sub> is set speed in m/s; v is actual speed in m/s; u is throttle command (0 to 100 %); K<sub>p</sub> is proportional gain in % per (m/s); K<sub>i</sub> is integral gain in % per m, since ∫e dt is in m; t is time in s.

The P term gives an immediate response. The I term sums error over time. On a hill, a plain P controller leaves a steady error: uphill needs more throttle, and the only way a P controller makes more throttle is to keep a positive error. The integral keeps adding while error exists, until error returns to zero. On downhill, the integral unwinds. If the car still goes faster than set, basic cruise cannot brake; it has throttle authority only.

ACC adds a forward sensor, usually a 77 GHz radar or a camera, and a gap loop. Radar measures distance d in metres to the lead car and relative speed. Target selection picks the nearest car in the host's own lane, the in-path target; the camera and the yaw rate help decide which lane each car is in.
tgap = d ÷ v; dtarget = ttarget × v; egap = d − dtarget; closing rate = v − vlead

t<sub>gap</sub> is time gap in s; d is measured distance to lead car in m; v is host speed in m/s; t<sub>target</sub> is selected time gap in s; d<sub>target</sub> is desired distance in m; e<sub>gap</sub> is gap error in m; v<sub>lead</sub> is lead car speed in m/s.

Time gap is in seconds, not metres. The driver selects t<sub>target</sub>, often 1.5 to 2.5 s. At a higher speed the same time gap needs a larger distance, so d<sub>target</sub> grows with v. A positive e<sub>gap</sub> means the host is farther than target; a negative e<sub>gap</sub> means it is closer and must slow. Closing rate is positive when the gap is shrinking.

The controller combines speed error and gap error. If the gap is large, it follows set speed. As the gap falls, it reduces speed; if needed it applies the service brakes through the ESP hydraulic unit. Basic cruise has no brake authority. A car cutting in makes d drop suddenly; the controller brakes, but if the cut-in is too close the driver must brake. Stop-and-go ACC can brake to zero and restart. The brake pedal always cancels or overrides; the accelerator can also override. Sensor fusion is in ADAS; PI tuning is in PI and PD controllers.

figure.caption: The ACC gap of the worked example. The lead car is 60 m ahead, 10 m beyond the 50 m target; if nothing changes the gap closes in 12 s, while a steady 1.25 m/s² brake settles the host at 20 m/s and 50 m after 4 s.

examples.question: A host car is set to 25 m/s. Its 77 GHz radar sees a lead car in the same lane travelling at 20 m/s at a distance of 60 m. The driver has selected a 2.0 s time gap. (a) Find the present time gap. (b) Find the target distance. (c) Find the gap error. (d) Find the closing rate. (e) At the present speeds, how long before the gap would become zero if nothing changed? (f) What constant deceleration of the host, starting now, brings it down to the lead car's 20 m/s exactly when the gap reaches the 50 m target, and how long does that take?
steps: Present time gap: t<sub>gap</sub> = d ÷ v<sub>host</sub> = 60 m ÷ 25 m/s = 2.4 s.
Target distance: d<sub>target</sub> = t<sub>target</sub> × v<sub>host</sub> = 2.0 s × 25 m/s = 50 m.
Gap error: e<sub>gap</sub> = d − d<sub>target</sub> = 60 m − 50 m = +10 m. The host is 10 m farther than target.
Closing rate: v<sub>host</sub> − v<sub>lead</sub> = 25 m/s − 20 m/s = 5 m/s. Positive, so the gap is shrinking.
Time to zero gap at present speeds: t = d ÷ closing rate = 60 m ÷ 5 m/s = 12 s. This is the time-to-collision, TTC. The target gap itself would be reached in (60 − 50) ÷ 5 = 2 s.
The closing speed must fall from 5 m/s to 0 while the gap shrinks by 10 m (from 60 m to 50 m). In relative motion, a = closing² ÷ (2 × 10 m) = 5² ÷ 20 = 1.25 m/s², and the time is 5 ÷ 1.25 = 4 s.
Check: in 4 s the host covers 25 × 4 − ½ × 1.25 × 4² = 90 m and the lead car 20 × 4 = 80 m, so the gap becomes 60 − (90 − 80) = 50 m, and the host speed is 25 − 1.25 × 4 = 20 m/s.
examples.answer: Time gap 2.4 s, target distance 50 m, gap error +10 m, closing rate 5 m/s, time to zero gap (TTC) 12 s; a steady 1.25 m/s² of braking for 4 s settles the host at 20 m/s and 50 m behind.
examples.check:
v_host, v_lead, d, t_target = 25, 20, 60, 2.0
t_gap = d / v_host
d_target = t_target * v_host
e_gap = d - d_target
closing = v_host - v_lead
ttc = d / closing
a = closing**2 / (2 * e_gap)
t = closing / a
gap = d - ((v_host * t - 0.5 * a * t * t) - v_lead * t)
print(t_gap, d_target, e_gap, closing, ttc, a, t, gap, v_host - a * t)

traps: Basic cruise control cannot brake; it only moves the throttle. On a long downhill the car can exceed set speed.
Time gap is in seconds, not metres. The target distance changes with speed: 2.0 s is 50 m at 25 m/s but 40 m at 20 m/s.
Set speed is not actual speed while the loop is catching up. The error is v<sub>set</sub> − v, not v<sub>set</sub> alone.
Gap error sign matters. Positive e<sub>gap</sub> means the host is farther than target, not closer.
The brake pedal always overrides ACC. ACC brake force comes through the service brakes and ESP, not from a separate pedal.

quiz.q: What does the SET button store in basic cruise control?
quiz.a: It stores the current speed as v<sub>set</sub>, the set speed.

quiz.q: Name two forward sensors used by ACC.
Why does a PI controller need the integral term to hold speed on a hill?
quiz.a: A P controller needs a steady error to make extra throttle. Uphill, that leaves the car slower than set. The integral sums the error and keeps increasing throttle until the error becomes zero.

quiz.q: A host car is set to 30 m/s. The lead car is at 24 m/s and 72 m away. The selected time gap is 2.0 s. Find the time gap, target distance, gap error and closing rate.
quiz.a: t<sub>gap</sub> = 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4 s. d<sub>target</sub> = 2.0 × 30 = 60 m. e<sub>gap</sub> = 72 − 60 = +12 m. Closing rate = 30 − 24 = 6 m/s.

quiz.q: A basic cruise control car speeds up above the set speed on a long downhill. Why can it not correct this?
quiz.a: Basic cruise has throttle authority only. It can close the throttle, but gravity can still push the car faster. Without brake authority it cannot remove the extra speed.

quiz.q: A car cuts in 15 m ahead while ACC is set at 25 m/s with a 2.0 s target gap. Why might ACC fail to avoid a collision?
quiz.a: The time gap is 15 ÷ 25 = 0.6 s against a 2.0 s target, so the gap error is 15 − 50 = −35 m at short range. The needed deceleration may exceed the brake command, and the sensor may not confirm the new target in time. The driver must brake.

quiz.q: What does pressing the brake pedal do to ACC?
quiz.a: It cancels or overrides ACC immediately.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ACC uses radar and camera fusion, and the gap loop is often model predictive control rather than a simple PI loop. Stop-and-go systems must hold the car on a slope without rolling, so they share work with the electronic parking brake. Search for adaptive cruise control time gap, radar-camera fusion and stop-and-go ACC.
